strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem (length bias/reward hacking in RLHF) and clearly identifies a limitation of prior work—the linear length-reward assumption—that is worth challenging.

The proposed FiMi-RM framework is reasonably intuitive: decoupling reward from length by learning a flexible non-linear fitting model (length encoding + ResNet) rather than assuming linearity, and then using a correlation-based debiasing loss to remove that learned dependency from the reward model.

The paper provides fairly comprehensive empirical validation across multiple angles: preference-dataset accuracy split by C-longer/R-longer, length-reward scatter/binned plots, downstream alignment via both BoN and DPO, length-controlled AlpacaEval, and length distribution/histogram analyses of selected and DPO-annotated responses.

The qualitative analysis of the fitted length-reward curve (strong linear regime for short responses, decelerating for medium, and noisy for long responses) is an interesting empirical observation that could be useful to the community even independent of the debiasing method itself.
Comparisons against a reasonable baseline (ODIN) and vanilla RM lend some context to the results.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on only a single dataset (Anthropic HH-derived Dahoas-rm-static) and GPT-4-based Alpaca-Eval judging references generated from the same small-ish SFT model; no results on more standard/larger benchmarks (e.g., UltraFeedback, TL;DR, Reddit, standard AlpacaEval leaderboard) or multiple preference datasets, which limits generalizability claims.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or repeated runs are reported for any of the tables (accuracy, LC-WR, WR); given that reported differences between FiMi-RM and ODIN/vanilla RM are often small (e.g., 1-2 points in LC-WR), it's unclear whether these differences are meaningful or within noise.

The accuracy table shows FiMi-RM has *lower* overall RM accuracy than both baselines on both model sizes (69.00 vs 70.83/70.31 for 7B), and the paper's justification (that this reflects a fairer length-balanced evaluation) is plausible but not rigorously established—e.g., no analysis of whether the R-longer subset itself contains more inherently low-quality-but-longer chosen responses, or whether the drop stems from genuinely lost preference-modeling capacity rather than bias removal.

The method introduces a fairly complex three-stage, alternating-training pipeline (with several hyperparameters: encoding dimension d=32, alternation frequency a=8, ResNet depth) but provides no ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual design choices (length encoding vs. raw length input, Pearson-only vs. MSE-only loss, ResNet vs. simpler MLP, alternation frequency sensitivity), making it hard to assess necessity/robustness of each component.

No comparison to other recent non-linear or post-hoc debiasing baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., Huang et al.'s local linear regression approach, Shen et al.'s Product-of-Experts approach), only to ODIN and vanilla RM, weakening the comparative evidence for superiority.

The claim of a 'multiphase' length-reward relation (linear-sublinear-noisy) is drawn from visual inspection of a single fitted curve on one dataset/model with no quantitative characterization (e.g., changepoint detection, confidence intervals) or replication across models/datasets, so the generalizability of this finding is unclear.

Models used (Qwen2.5-7B/1.5B) are relatively small and only two sizes are tested; no discussion of whether findings hold at scale or transfer to more modern/larger reward model setups, which are increasingly standard in current RLHF research.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: exact code/model release is not mentioned, and some pipeline details (e.g., exact ResNet architecture, multi-GPU aggregation specifics for Pearson computation, LR/scheduler for the fitting model) are described somewhat tersely, which could hinder faithful reproduction.

The DPO setup (reannotating a held-out set using different RMs, then training DPO on the relabeled data) is somewhat unconventional and could introduce confounds (e.g., relabeling noise, dataset size effects) that are not analyzed separately from the RM's inherent quality.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem in RLHF: the failure of linear-relation assumptions in existing length-debiasing methods.
The proposed three-stage pipeline (warm-up, bias fitting with length encoding + ResNet, decorrelation-based debiasing) is clearly described with explicit loss formulations.

Multiple complementary analyses are presented (subset accuracy, length-reward scatter plots, downstream DPO/BoN win rates, length distribution histograms, training-curve visualization of the fitted bias), giving a reasonably broad (if shallow) empirical picture.
The qualitative finding of a multi-phase (linear/sublinear/noisy) length-reward relationship is an interesting observation that could motivate future non-linear debiasing work.
weaknesses: Critically weak baseline comparison: the paper's central claim is that non-linear fitting is superior to linear-relation assumptions used in prior work (length penalty [41], Product-of-Experts [40], Huang et al. regression-based calibration [19]), yet none of these directly relevant linear baselines are actually implemented or compared against—only ODIN (a different, two-head architecture) is used as a baseline, leaving the paper's core comparative claim empirically unsupported.

Single dataset (Anthropic HH-rlhf static split) and only two closely related model scales (Qwen2.5-7B/1.5B) are used; there is no evidence the method generalizes to other preference datasets (e.g., summarization, UltraFeedback) or larger/other model families.

No error bars, variance estimates, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported anywhere; several reported improvements (e.g., Table 3 DPO LC-WR for Qwen2.5-1.5B: 73.84 vs 73.68/73.22) are small enough to plausibly fall within noise, undermining confidence that the method's benefits are real rather than incidental.

No ablation studies isolating the contributions of individual design choices (length encoding vs. raw scalar input, ResNet vs. simpler MLP, Pearson+MSE combined loss vs. either alone, alternating-training schedule with step size a=8), so it is unclear which components actually drive the reported gains.
Key hyperparameters (embedding dimension d=32, alternation interval a=8) are stated without justification or sensitivity analysis, weakening reproducibility and interpretability.

PPO, the canonical RLHF optimization algorithm, is explicitly excluded from evaluation, so the method is validated only on BoN and DPO (the latter requiring an unusual re-annotation procedure whose validity as a faithful proxy for standard DPO/RLHF is not established).

Evaluation relies solely on GPT-4-as-judge via length-controlled Alpaca-Eval with no human evaluation, and no details are given on the number of trials or judge consistency, raising reliability concerns given known instability of automated LLM judges.

The claimed accuracy trade-off (Table 1: overall accuracy drops from 70.83% to 69.00%) is rationalized narratively but not quantitatively justified as an acceptable cost, and the reduction could partly reflect degraded general preference-modeling capability rather than pure debiasing.

The theoretical justification for using Pearson-correlation minimization as a debiasing objective is weak: removing linear correlation does not guarantee removal of non-linear or causal length dependence, which is somewhat in tension with the paper's own emphasis on non-linearity.
No code or training artifacts are indicated as released, and given the intricate multi-stage alternating training procedure, reproducibility solely from the paper's description is uncertain.

strengths: Addresses a well-recognized and practically important problem in RLHF (length bias/reward hacking), motivated with clear examples of prior work's limitations (no bias characterization, or linear-only assumptions).

The proposed three-stage pipeline (warm-up, non-linear bias fitting via a lightweight ResNet-based model, and decoupling via Pearson-correlation minimization) is a reasonably novel way to move beyond the linear length-reward assumption used by prior methods like ODIN and Length Penalty.

Extensive empirical validation: two base model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B), two primary alignment algorithms (DPO, BoN) plus additional SimPO and GRPO results in the appendix, several benchmarks (length-controlled AlpacaEval, MT-Bench, IFEval), and a second training dataset (RLHFlow) for generalization checks.

Reasonably thorough ablation study covering joint vs. multi-stage training, alternating vs. non-alternating updates, and multiple fitting-model architectures (linear, polynomial, CNN, MLP vs. ResNet), which helps justify design choices.

Useful diagnostic visualizations (length-reward scatter plots, BoN selection length distributions, DPO chosen/rejected length gaps, fitted curve evolution) that make the qualitative claims about reduced length bias easier to verify.
Includes a computational cost analysis showing the added fitting model does not meaningfully increase training time, supporting practical applicability.
Thoughtful discussion in the limitations section acknowledging that length and human preference are not necessarily fully independent, which shows appropriate scientific caution.
weaknesses: The core debiasing mechanism relies on minimizing the Pearson correlation between the reward and the fitted model's output; despite the paper's claim that this does not assume linearity, Pearson correlation is fundamentally a linear-dependence measure, so achieving near-zero correlation does not guarantee that non-linear/higher-order length dependence has been removed from the reward model itself (only that it doesn't correlate linearly with the fitted curve). This leaves a logical gap between the stated goal (non-linear debiasing) and the actual optimization objective.

Primary experiments rely on a single, relatively small and dated dataset (Dahoas-rm-static, 30k RM training samples); while RLHFlow is used as a secondary generalization check, broader coverage across more diverse/larger preference datasets would strengthen claims of general applicability.
No standard PPO evaluation is included (justified by computational cost), which limits the completeness of the RLHF picture, since PPO remains a common deployment setting for reward models.

Evaluation depends entirely on GPT-4/automatic judges (AlpacaEval, MT-Bench) with no human evaluation, which is a known-imperfect proxy especially for a paper specifically about mitigating evaluator/annotator length bias.

Results are reported as single-run point estimates without variance or significance testing across seeds, making it hard to assess how robust the reported improvements (often a few points in LC-WR) are to run-to-run variability.

Comparison baselines are limited to Vanilla RM, Length Penalty, and ODIN; several other more recent length-debiasing methods discussed in related work (e.g., RRM, ALBM, SamPO, Park et al.) are not empirically compared despite being readily available, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art performance.

The interpretation of the accuracy trade-off in Table 1 (drop in C-longer accuracy framed as removal of a length 'shortcut' rather than capability loss) is argued qualitatively rather than being verified with an independent, length-controlled ground-truth quality measure.

strengths: The problem (length bias / reward hacking in RLHF reward models) is well-motivated and clearly situated within existing literature, with a reasonably thorough related-work discussion distinguishing linear-assumption approaches (ODIN, length penalty) from bias-form-agnostic approaches (RRM, KL regularization).

The experimental protocol is fairly broad: two base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B), two primary alignment algorithms (DPO, BoN), and additional appendix experiments across SimPO, GRPO, and a second dataset (RLHFlow), which helps demonstrate some generality of the proposed effect.

Extensive ablations are provided (joint vs. multi-stage training, alternating schedule, fitting-model architecture choices) along with a computational cost analysis showing the added fitting model incurs negligible overhead.

The paper includes multiple complementary diagnostics beyond win-rate numbers (length-reward scatter plots, BoN selection length distributions, chosen/rejected length gaps in DPO annotation), which together paint a consistent qualitative picture of reduced length bias.
weaknesses: Central methodological tension: the paper's core claim is that length bias is non-linear and previous linear-correlation-based methods are inadequate, yet the actual debiasing objective (Eq. 5–6) minimizes the Pearson correlation |ρ(r, r̂_sg)| between the reward and the fitting model's output — a strictly linear correlation measure. Minimizing linear correlation between r and a nonlinear function of length does not guarantee removal of the nonlinear length dependence in r itself; the paper does not provide theoretical or empirical justification (e.g., mutual information, HSIC, or distance correlation analysis) that this objective actually achieves the claimed nonlinear decoupling, undermining the central contribution.

The reward-model accuracy results (Table 1) show an overall accuracy drop for FiMi-RM relative to baselines on both models, explained post hoc via the C-longer/R-longer subset argument. This explanation, while plausible, is not independently validated (e.g., via synthetic length-bias injection with known ground truth, or human-labeled quality-controlled subsets), leaving the interpretation partly speculative.

Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4-as-judge (AlpacaEval, length-controlled win rate) and MT-Bench (also LLM-judged), which are themselves documented to carry stylistic/length biases; no human evaluation is included to corroborate that the debiased model's outputs are genuinely higher quality rather than differently styled. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the win-rate differences, which are typically noisy metrics, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (often a few points) are robust.

Ablation results for the fitting-model architecture (Table 5) show only marginal differences between Linear (71.67), MLP (71.35), 1D-CNN (71.15), and ResNet (72.59), which weakens the claim that explicitly modeling non-linearity is critical to the method's success, since a simple linear fit performs nearly as well.

Main experiments rely on a single, relatively small preference dataset (Anthropic HH static split, 30k RM training pairs); broader validation is relegated to a brief appendix result on one additional dataset, limiting confidence in generalizability across more diverse and realistic RLHF preference distributions.

Baseline implementation details (e.g., the length-penalty coefficient, ODIN hyperparameters) are not reported, making it difficult to assess whether baselines were adequately tuned for a fair comparison.

The rise in Bradley-Terry loss during Stage 3 (0.530→0.566) is interpreted as evidence the length shortcut was removed, but this argument is circular without an independent measure of preference-modeling quality (e.g., a length-balanced held-out human-labeled test set) to confirm the model still tracks genuine preferences rather than simply becoming a worse discriminator.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem in RLHF (length bias in reward models) and clearly differentiates itself from prior linear-assumption approaches (ODIN, Length Penalty) and non-characterized-bias approaches (RRM, KL regularization).

The three-stage design (warm-up, bias fitting, debiasing) is intuitive and the use of a lightweight, cheap fitting model to explicitly model the length-reward relation is a reasonable and relatively novel technical contribution.

Extensive empirical validation: two base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B), two main alignment algorithms (DPO, BoN) plus additional experiments with SimPO and GRPO, and an additional dataset (RLHFlow) in the appendix, showing consistent improvements in LC-WR/WR and reduced verbosity.

Thorough ablation study covering joint vs. multi-stage training, alternating vs. non-alternating updates, and multiple fitting-model architectures (linear, polynomial, CNN, MLP, ResNet), which strengthens confidence in specific design choices.

Good supplementary analyses: length-reward scatter plots, BoN selection length distributions, DPO chosen/rejected length gaps, fitting-curve visualization over training steps, and a computational cost analysis, all of which support the central claim with converging evidence.
The paper is transparent about the accuracy trade-off on the C-longer/R-longer split and offers a plausible explanation (removal of length shortcut) rather than hiding the result.
Sufficient implementation detail (hyperparameters, hardware, network structure in the appendix) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core training objective for the fitting model maximizes the (absolute) Pearson correlation coefficient between the fitted output and the reward, rather than a standard regression loss (e.g., MSE) toward E[reward|length]. Since Pearson correlation is invariant to affine transforms and does not uniquely pin down a conditional expectation, it is unclear why this objective correctly recovers the true non-linear bias curve rather than any curve highly correlated with reward; no ablation compares this choice against a direct regression loss, despite it being the paper's central technical innovation.

Similarly, the debiasing stage minimizes |ρ(r, r̂_sg)| computed over a batch, which decorrelates linearly at the batch level; this may not guarantee removal of the specific non-linear dependency structure that was fitted, and batch-level Pearson estimates (even aggregated across 8 GPUs) could be noisy/unstable as a training signal.

No variance/error-bar reporting or multiple-run analysis; all comparisons (Tables 1-4, ablations, appendix results) appear to be single runs, making it hard to assess whether the reported gaps (often 1-4 points in LC-WR) are statistically meaningful versus training noise.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow: only ODIN and Length Penalty are used as empirical baselines, while several methods discussed in related work as directly relevant (e.g., Huang et al.'s local linear regression, Shen et al.'s Product-of-Experts decoupling, RRM's causal framework) are not empirically compared, despite being explicitly positioned as competing approaches in the introduction.

Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4-based judges (AlpacaEval, MT-Bench) which themselves are documented to exhibit length bias; while LC-WR partially mitigates this, the interaction between the evaluator's own bias and the phenomenon under study is not deeply discussed.

The reduced overall preference-accuracy (Table 1) is explained qualitatively as an artifact of discarding the length shortcut, but this claim is not independently validated (e.g., no held-out quality-only or length-matched accuracy benchmark) beyond the downstream win-rate improvements, leaving some ambiguity about how much genuine preference signal correlated with length may have been discarded alongside the spurious bias.

The fitting model depends only on length and is agnostic to content, so it necessarily targets marginal length bias rather than any residual bias conditioned on response quality; the practical significance of this modeling choice relative to alternatives is not deeply analyzed.

The paper's claimed 25% training-time reduction stems from allocating a large fraction of steps to cheap fitting-model-only updates rather than RM updates; while wall-clock time is indeed reduced, this framing partially obscures that the reward model itself receives fewer gradient updates than the vanilla baseline within an epoch, which could confound comparison of statistical efficiency.
